## Definition

A **non-directional hypothesis** (two-tailed) predicts that there will be a difference or relationship between variables, but does not specify the direction of that effect.

## Key Characteristics

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| No direction specified | Just predicts "a difference" |
| Two-tailed test | Critical regions in both tails |
| More conservative | Harder to reach significance |
| More flexible | Can detect effects in either direction |

## Examples

| Non-directional | Directional |
|-----------------|-------------|
| "There will be **a difference** in scores between groups" | "Group A will score **higher**" |
| "Caffeine will **affect** memory" | "Caffeine will **improve** memory" |
| "Age will be **related to** reaction time" | "Age will be **positively related to** reaction time" |

## When to Use Non-directional Hypotheses

Use when:

- No strong theoretical basis for direction
- Previous research shows mixed results
- Both directions are theoretically possible
- You want to detect effects in either direction

## Two-Tailed Testing

```
Two-tailed test (α = .05):

        ┌──2.5%──┐         ┌──2.5%──┐
        │░░░░░░░░│         │░░░░░░░░│
────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────
       -1.96     0        +1.96
       ← Reject H₀ →      ← Reject H₀ →

Significant if result falls in EITHER tail
```

## Advantages and Disadvantages

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|------------|---------------|
| Detects effects in either direction | Less statistical power |
| More conservative | Higher critical value |
| Safer when direction uncertain | May miss real effects |

## Choosing Between Directional and Non-directional

| Consideration | Directional | Non-directional |
|---------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Theory | Strong prediction | Uncertain direction |
| Prior research | Consistent findings | Mixed findings |
| Interest | One direction only | Either direction |
| Default | Less common | More common |

## DataLab Connection

For **Sixth Sense**, a non-directional hypothesis may be appropriate: "There will be a significant relationship between belief in intuition and prediction accuracy" (because we don't know if believers will be better or worse).
